claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially has a homogeneous high-temperature BCC structure.
Isothermal annealing near 700 °C promotes gradual chemical short-range-order development in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Longer annealing durations from 1 to 100 hours will produce progressively more SRO.
SRO clusters or locally ordered BCC regions act as precursors to ordered-phase nucleation.
SRO changes local chemical potentials in the BCC phase.
The SRO-induced change in local chemical potentials lowers the nucleation-energy barrier for ordered secondary phases.
B2 or L21 phases are candidate ordered secondary phases in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Pre-annealed samples will form ordered secondary phases more readily during cooling or subsequent thermal exposure than directly quenched samples.
Longer subcritical annealing will increase the XRD intensity and volume fraction of ordered secondary phases relative to the directly quenched baseline.
The development of ordered secondary phases will be visible by TEM.
The annealing-induced structural changes will be accompanied by changes in mechanical properties.
Samples directly quenched from the high-temperature state without an isothermal hold will remain predominantly homogeneous BCC.
Sufficient atomic mobility at moderate annealing temperatures and accessible times is required for SRO development.
Very brief exposure or kinetic limitations can prevent development of SRO.
Very rapid quenching can prevent SRO formation.
Oxidation can dominate or interfere with the phase-transformation behavior unless atmospheric effects are minimized.
XRD, TEM, and APT can respectively assess ordered-phase fraction, local ordering and morphology, and atomic-scale chemical ordering.
A lack of statistically significant increases in both SRO indicators and ordered-phase abundance after extended annealing would falsify the proposed SRO-mediated nucleation mechanism.

contradictions.description: The intervention uses rapid quenching after annealing, whereas the conditions and boundary fields say very rapid quenching can prevent SRO and make the mechanism inapplicable. This can be reconciled if SRO forms during the hold and quenching merely preserves it, but that distinction is not stated clearly.
